discovery: The optical lattice clock: atomic timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision metrology
motivation: Katori proposed trapping neutral atoms in an optical lattice at a 'magic wavelength', where the light shifts of both clock states cancel. This went against the common view that a trap would always spoil a clock transition. It combines the long interrogation times of trapped ions with the signal-to-noise of thousands of atoms. Katori's group first demonstrated the scheme with strontium. Ye turned it into the most precise measuring instrument ever built. His group used frequency combs and ultrastable lasers to reach 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, resolve the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample, and explore many-body interactions in the clock itself. Optical lattice clocks have led to a planned redefinition of the SI second. They enable relativistic geodesy and serve as probes of dark matter and of variation in the fundamental constants. They are a clear case of fundamental quantum control of atoms becoming a transformative measurement technology.
